metadata.title: Boris Cherny: We Cut 80% of Claude Code's Prompt
metadata.speaker: Boris Cherny (creator of Claude Code, guest), Forrest (Y Combinator, interviewer)

executive_takeaway: (1) Anthropic deleted 80% of Claude Code's system prompt for Opus 5 because a more intelligent model no longer needs instructions correcting behavior it now does natively — the harness is rebuilt from near-scratch with every model generation via 'ablation.' (2) Opus 5 combined with 'auto mode' appears effectively non-prompt-injectable, via three layers: an aligned model, a prompt-injection classifier built on mechanistic-interpretability neuron detection, and an auto-mode classifier. (3) The core skill for builders is 'un-hobbling' the model, i.e. removing product/harness friction that stops the model from doing what it's already capable of — this is literally the origin story of Claude Code (giving Sonnet 3.5 full terminal access instead of IDE autocomplete). (4) Boris had Claude rewrite Bun's entire JavaScript runtime from Zig to Rust — ~100k+ lines, one prompt plus steering, using a 'dynamic workflow,' running for 11 days, now in production; a task that would previously have taken well over a year. (5) Anthropic now runs dozens of autonomous 'routines' (loops running in the cloud) that maintain their own codebases daily: deleting dead code, shipping/removing finished experiments, writing missing tests, deleting useless tests, and unifying duplicated abstractions ('abstraction police') — hundreds to thousands of agents running per day. (6) Practical advice for builders: give Claude harder tasks than you think it can handle, describe the goal/guardrails/exit criteria (not step-by-step instructions), and above all give it a way to verify its own work — verification, not prompting, is what separates top users. (7) Boris predicts 'coding is solved' for his kind of coding, but not yet for deep systems code, distributed systems, or pixel-perfect UI verification.

conviction_map.action_status: DID IT — cut 80% of Claude Code's system prompt for Opus 5
conviction_map.core_thesis: Every new model release, Anthropic deletes large parts of the system prompt/tools and re-adds only what the model still demonstrably needs, via ablation (delete everything, add back line by line). Opus 5 is intelligent enough that most prior corrective prompting is now dead weight, and the model performs slightly better without it.
conviction_map.risks: Bare model without product prompts behaves less predictably for end users; some prompt scaffolding is still needed for product-grade UX

conviction_map.action_status: CLAIMS NOT YET DEMONSTRATED IN THE WILD
conviction_map.core_thesis: Combining a well-aligned model (~3 years of alignment research) with a prompt-injection classifier (based on mechanistic interpretability — detecting neurons that fire on injection) and an auto-mode classifier means the team 'cannot demonstrate prompt injection anymore' on Opus 5, a marked jump from Opus 4.7/4.8 and Sonnet 5.
conviction_map.risks: Internal team framing, not independently audited; 'cannot demonstrate' is not the same as 'immune'; adversaries continually probe for new injection vectors

conviction_map.topic: Dynamic Workflows for Massive Test-Time Compute
conviction_map.action_status: IN PRODUCTION — used to rewrite Bun from Zig to Rust in 11 days
conviction_map.core_thesis: Dynamic workflows orchestrate an 'algebra for agents' (sequential + parallel composition) inside a Bun-based sandbox VM, letting a single prompt spawn and coordinate thousands of agents across multiple staged passes (build, verify, summarize, fan out again). Framed as a new axis of test-time compute scaling beyond model size/data/training flops.
conviction_map.risks: Requires steering, not fully one-shot; cost/token usage at that scale is non-trivial; still early and under-documented externally

conviction_map.action_status: IN PRODUCTION — dozens of routines run daily across CLI, iOS, Android, desktop apps
conviction_map.core_thesis: Cloud-based 'routines' (cron-like, can run without a laptop open) now handle dead-code cleanup, retiring finished experiments, adding missing test coverage, deleting low-value tests, and unifying duplicated abstractions — hundreds to thousands of agents/day, doing work Boris compares to 'dozens or hundreds of engineers.'
conviction_map.risks: Not fully automated yet ('not totally there'); autonomous refactors/deletions carry inherent risk of removing something still needed if verification is imperfect

technology_ai_views.theme: System-prompt ablation as standard harness-building practice
technology_ai_views.view: Delete the entire system prompt on every new model release, add lines back one at a time only when the model repeatedly and demonstrably needs them; treat this as an eval, not a guess.
technology_ai_views.why: Prevents prompt bloat from accumulating corrective instructions the newer model no longer needs; keeps the harness lean and the model's native intelligence unobstructed.

technology_ai_views.theme: Product overhang / un-hobbling as the core opportunity for AI startups
technology_ai_views.view: Every model generation can already do things almost no product lets it fully express; the founder opportunity is building the harness/product that removes that friction, not training new capability.
technology_ai_views.companies: Claude Code (origin story), general applicability to any AI product
technology_ai_views.why: Named as the literal genesis of Claude Code (Sonnet 3.5 + full terminal access vs. prior IDE autocomplete/chat-only tools) and framed as still wide open today.

technology_ai_views.theme: Model routing / language-to-language full codebase rewrites
technology_ai_views.view: Modern models can now rewrite an entire codebase from one language to another (e.g., Zig to Rust) given a good test suite to verify against — a capability that did not exist reliably even ~1 model generation ago.
technology_ai_views.why: Demonstrates 'product overhang': tasks previously requiring a year+ of senior engineering time compressed to 11 days of largely autonomous agent work.

technology_ai_views.theme: Prompt engineering giving way to task design + verification
technology_ai_views.view: The differentiating skill is no longer crafting the perfect prompt but (a) giving Claude a task slightly harder than expected, and (b) building in a way for it to verify its own output (tests, screenshots, pixel diffs, MCP context) so it doesn't get stuck.
technology_ai_views.companies: General — Claude Code, Claude Desktop (Electron→Swift rewrite example), Claude in Slack ('Claude tag')
technology_ai_views.why: Reframes what 'top 1% Claude users' actually do differently from casual users.

ai_workflows.name: Dynamic Workflows (large-scale multi-stage agent orchestration)
ai_workflows.goal: Handle a single large, multi-stage task (full codebase rewrite, deep data analysis, complex multi-PR feature) by fanning out to many agents in coordinated stages.
ai_workflows.tools: Claude Code 'dynamic workflow' feature, Bun-based sandbox VM
ai_workflows.approach: Just say 'use a workflow' — Claude triggers it. Agents run a first pass, a second stage verifies/summarizes, a third stage may fan out again; run in sequence or in parallel like a composable agent algebra.
ai_workflows.why: Lets one prompt productively orchestrate dozens to thousands of agents instead of one linear conversation, dramatically raising effective test-time compute on hard tasks.

ai_workflows.name: Loops and Routines (recurring autonomous maintenance)
ai_workflows.goal: Run a repetitive, non-context-sharing task on a schedule (hourly/daily) without a human present.
ai_workflows.tools: Claude Code 'loop' (local cron-like) or 'routine' (cloud-based, laptop can be closed)
ai_workflows.approach: Write one single-sentence prompt (e.g., 'clean up dead code across all codebases') and let Claude run it daily; it derives its own methodology (static + dynamic analysis) and opens a PR each run.
ai_workflows.why: Anthropic now runs dozens of these routines across CLI/iOS/Android/desktop, doing continuous codebase maintenance that used to require dedicated engineer time.

ai_workflows.name: Verify-driven task delegation for long-running/large tasks
ai_workflows.goal: Get a model to complete a task 'too hard' for it to one-shot without micromanaging every step.
ai_workflows.tools: Any Claude surface (Code, Desktop, Claude tag/Slack)
ai_workflows.approach: Describe the goal, guardrails, and exit criteria at a high level (not a numbered step-by-step); give the model a concrete way to verify its own work (a test suite, a screenshot-and-pixel-diff loop, an MCP for missing context); let it run — sometimes for days to weeks — and check back periodically.
ai_workflows.why: Example: rewriting the Claude Desktop Electron app in Swift by having the agent run the Electron app in a Mac VM, screenshot it, and pixel-compare against the Swift rewrite in a loop — running continuously for 2+ weeks unattended.

notable_quotes.quote: We deleted 80% of the system prompt. You can actually try deleting the rest of it, too.
notable_quotes.speaker: Boris Cherny
notable_quotes.context: On the Opus 5 Claude Code release and the practice of aggressively trimming the system prompt each model generation.

notable_quotes.quote: For people that aren't building agentic products, but you're using Claude code, every 6 months delete your Claude MD. Delete your skills. Delete your hooks. See what the model does and it might surprise you.
notable_quotes.speaker: Boris Cherny
notable_quotes.context: Advice to regular Claude Code users, not just harness builders, on periodically stripping accumulated customization.

notable_quotes.quote: You have to take the time to get to know it and then adjust the harness based on that... it's just very much like an empirical and kind of scientific thing.
notable_quotes.speaker: Boris Cherny
notable_quotes.context: Comparing model-generation harness building to working with a living creature rather than doing traditional up-front system design.

notable_quotes.quote: It ran for 11 days, and it rewrote the entire code base.
notable_quotes.speaker: Boris Cherny
notable_quotes.context: On having Claude rewrite Bun's runtime from Zig to Rust — a task he estimates would have taken well over a year with human engineers.

notable_quotes.quote: I think people tend to overthink it a little bit... trying to over specify and trying to be overly specific and then get the model to do the task exactly the way that you would have done it — that's just not the way the model works.
notable_quotes.speaker: Boris Cherny
notable_quotes.context: On the most common failure mode among experienced engineers new to agentic coding.

notable_quotes.quote: Coding is solved for the kind of coding that I do. It's not solved for everyone.
notable_quotes.speaker: Boris Cherny
notable_quotes.context: Caveat on the 'coding is solved' claim — deep systems code, distributed systems, and pixel-perfect UI verification are named as still-weak areas.

risks: Prompt-injection resistance claims ('we cannot demonstrate prompt injection anymore') come from the team that built the classifier and are self-reported, not third-party audited — worth independent red-teaming before relying on it for high-stakes autonomous agents.
The 11-day Bun Zig-to-Rust rewrite involved human steering, not a true one-shot; the framing 'it just went' understates how much oversight large autonomous rewrites still require.
'Coding is solved' is explicitly caveated by Boris himself — deep systems code, distributed systems, and pixel-level UI verification are named as areas where Claude still struggles.
Advice to 'delete your CLAUDE.md/skills/hooks every 6 months' assumes access to the latest frontier model (Opus 5); teams on older or smaller models may still need the removed scaffolding.

Transcript is from YouTube auto-captions and may contain minor transcription errors (e.g., model/product names); verify exact figures (agent counts, day counts) against a primary source before citing precisely.

actionable_takeaways.item: When adopting a new model version, don't tune your prompt/system message incrementally — delete it and rebuild from empirical evidence of where the model actually fails, adding lines back only when it repeatedly stumbles on the same thing.
Every ~6 months, try deleting your CLAUDE.md, skills, and hooks and see how the model performs without them — accumulated scaffolding may now be net-negative on a more capable model.
Give the model higher-level goals, guardrails, and exit criteria instead of granular step-by-step instructions — over-specifying is the most common failure mode among experienced engineers.
Build in a way for the model to verify its own work (tests, screenshot/pixel diffing, an MCP for missing context) before delegating a hard, long-running task — this matters more than prompt wording.

Look for 'product overhang' in your own domain: capabilities the current frontier model already has that no product yet fully exposes — this is presented as the actual founding insight behind Claude Code.

For repetitive, well-specified maintenance tasks (dead code cleanup, test coverage gaps, de-duplicating abstractions), a single-sentence prompt run on a recurring cloud routine can replace substantial ongoing engineering time.

Verify claims about prompt-injection immunity and agent counts (e.g., '11 days,' 'thousands of agents') independently before basing security or capacity decisions on them — these are anecdotal, self-reported figures from one interview.

other_notable_news.title: Opus 5 Reportedly Resists Prompt Injection via 3-Layer Defense
other_notable_news.detail: Boris describes combining an aligned model (years of alignment research), a mechanistic-interpretability-based prompt-injection classifier (detects specific 'injection' neurons), and an auto-mode classifier, claiming the team can no longer demonstrate prompt injection working against Opus 5 — a marked jump from Opus 4.7/4.8 and Sonnet 5.

other_notable_news.title: Periodically Delete Your Claude Customization Files
other_notable_news.detail: Boris recommends all Claude Code users — not just harness builders — delete CLAUDE.md, skills, and hooks roughly every 6 months (especially after a major model upgrade like Opus 5) to see if the model performs better without accumulated instructions.

other_notable_news.title: Boris Learned to Code on a TI-83 Calculator to Cheat on Math Tests
other_notable_news.detail: Boris's origin story: he taught himself BASIC on a TI-83 in middle school to build math solvers, wrote an internet guide on TI-83 programming, then learned assembly to build a calculus solver as the material got harder — framed as advice to learn CS by solving a real, practical problem first.

other_notable_news.title: Y Combinator Attendees Given Claude Max 20X Access
other_notable_news.detail: At the end of the talk, YC announced all attendees would receive Claude Max 20X access via a code sent by email.

glossary.definition: Research technique (borrowed for harness-building) of deleting a system prompt/component entirely, then re-adding pieces one at a time to measure each one's actual impact.
A Claude Code mode that lets the model run autonomously for very long stretches (days to months) without additional scaffolding like slash commands.

A safety layer that detects prompt-injection attempts using mechanistic-interpretability signals — specific neurons that activate when an injection is happening — combined with the auto-mode classifier.
The gap between what a model can already do and what the surrounding product lets it do; 'un-hobbling' means removing the product/harness friction that suppresses the model's real capability.
A Claude Code feature that lets a single prompt orchestrate large numbers of agents (sequential and parallel) inside a Bun sandbox VM for multi-stage, high-compute tasks.
Repeating scheduled Claude tasks — 'loop' runs locally (cron-like), 'routine' runs in the cloud so the task continues after the laptop is closed.
An open-source JavaScript runtime (a faster alternative to Node.js) that Claude Code is built on; originally written in Zig, later rewritten to Rust by Claude agents.
Anthropic's product for running Claude inside Slack.
Internal nickname for a routine that finds near-duplicated abstractions repeated across Anthropic's codebases and unifies them automatically.
